newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Peace a farce say Jews at Jerusalem bomb site.
newsitem.headline: Peace a farce say Jews at Jerusalem bomb site.

text.p: When an Israeli man spoke of peace at the scene of a double suicide bombing in Jerusalem on Wednesday, hordes of ultra-Orthodox Jews screamed at him to leave.
"We must continue the process or the enemies of peace will win," said Mike Masud, motioning behind him to the closed-off marketplace where two suicide bombers killed 12 people just hours before.
"Those who love peace will fight for it," he said as a crowd gathered.
"Peace is a nightmare," an ultra-Orthodox man shouted at him, waving his arms.
Masud smiled. "If you don't believe in it, it won't work," he said.
"I don't want more peace. I smelled the blood and the TNT," another man said, clenching his fists.
Masud raised his arms and backed away.
"I know what it's like to live with the Arabs. We can do that. We must live together. If peace won't work, we can always go for war. But we must try for peace first," he said.
Peace was not on the agenda for most of the ultra-Orthodox Jews who ventured to the market to gawk. Some pushed strollers with toddlers trailing behind.
Rubber gloves and plastic cups littered the gutters, crushed by hundreds of feet.
"We should kill them all," said one man, referring to Arabs.
"We need strong security. We need to restrict the Arabs and punish them severely, close all the borders," said Chaim Weiss, an ultra-Orthodox American Jew in Israel to study Jewish law.
"God must be mad, so many people die, innocent people," he said.
Even though Palestinian President Yasser Arafat condemned the bombing, few Jews at the market said they could ever trust Arabs.
"I think the poor, average Palestinian is being duped by Arafat like everyone else," said Rachel Rosenberg, 41, who immigrated to Israel from the United States seven years ago.
"(But) Arabs are not to be trusted. They've got the seeds of deception," she said.
"The Arabs, the young generation, are all being brought up to do suicide bombs," said a New Jersey man living in Israel.
"(For an Arab) it is a good deed to kill a Jew, it's a mitzvah (good deed). You cannot talk to them," said Rabbi Avraham Album, 70.
"I live in an area with Arabs and I know the Arabs," he said.
Despite all Masud's arguing, he couldn't change anyone's mind and eventually walked away from the crowd shaking his head.
"Every time something like this happens, extremists will say, 'Look, we're trying peace and look what we get.' Light must come to Israel," he said.
"It's very important to achieve justice, but most people don't believe in peace."
